common_name: Lady in Pink Fern (Rose-Pink-Stemmed Lady Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Lady in Pink carries rose-pink stems and midribs, a softer color companion to the red-stemmed Lady in Red.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and keep the soil from drying out, since lady fern wilts quickly in dry conditions and does not recover well from prolonged drought stress. Lady in Pink bears finely divided, lacy, light green fronds rising from distinctive rose-pink stems (stipes) and midribs (rachises), a softer, warmer color companion to the more common red-stemmed Lady in Red selection, and the pink coloring is most vivid on new spring growth. Its fine texture and colorful stems make it a good contrast plant among broader-leaved hostas and heucheras in a shaded border or woodland garden. Cut back tattered fronds in late winter before new growth emerges in spring, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Feather Falls Carex (Fine-Textured Weeping Green Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Feather Falls forms a dense, gracefully weeping mound of fine, bright green foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Feather Falls forms a dense, fountain-like mound of very fine, bright green, thread-like foliage that cascades gracefully over its edges, functioning almost like a miniature ornamental grass in shaded spots where true grasses struggle to perform. Its fine texture provides an excellent contrast to bold, broad-leaved shade perennials like hostas and heucheras, and works especially well spilling over the edge of a raised bed, container, or low wall. It tolerates both consistently moist soil and brief dry spells once established and is evergreen to semi-evergreen in milder climates, needing only an occasional light combing-out of tired old foliage in early spring to stay looking fresh.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Toffee Chip is a slower-spreading, more compact ajuga than older cultivars, better behaved in small borders.

directions: Plant in average, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; good drainage is important, since ajuga crowns can rot in constantly waterlogged soil despite the plant's general preference for moisture. Toffee Chip forms a low, dense mat of small, rounded leaves in a distinctive bronze-caramel color edged with a creamy border, a warmer, more muted palette than the deep purple or burgundy tones of older ajuga cultivars, with short spikes of blue flowers rising just above the foliage in spring. It spreads more slowly and stays more compact than many older, more aggressive ajuga cultivars, making it a better-behaved choice for small borders, rock gardens, and edging where a running groundcover could become a nuisance. It tolerates foot traffic lightly and needs little care beyond dividing and replanting congested patches every few years.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Atropurpurea is a classic older periwinkle selection with deep plum-purple flowers rather than the more common lavender-blue.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; established periwinkle tolerates dry shade and root competition from trees better than most groundcovers. Atropurpurea is a long-grown classic form of common periwinkle bearing deep, rich plum-purple flowers in spring, a distinctive departure from the pale lavender-blue of the species, held above trailing stems of small, glossy, deep green evergreen leaves that form a dense, weed-suppressing mat over time. It spreads steadily by rooting stems, making it useful for erosion control on shaded slopes and as a low-maintenance groundcover under trees where turf struggles. It needs essentially no care once established beyond an occasional edging to keep it within bounds, and shearing back hard every few years rejuvenates thin or leggy patches.

common_name: Christmas Tree Liriope (Cone-Shaped White-and-Lavender Flower Spikes)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Christmas Tree liriope is named for its distinctively cone-shaped flower spikes, wider at the base and tapering to a point.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; established clumps tolerate considerable drought and root competition from trees once settled in. Christmas Tree liriope forms tidy clumps of strappy, dark green, evergreen foliage and is named for its unusual flower spikes, which flare wider at the base and taper to a point in a distinct conical shape reminiscent of a small evergreen tree, opening white at the base and shading to soft lavender toward the tip in late summer. It makes a durable, low-maintenance edging or mass planting for shaded borders and pathways, spreading slowly into solid clumps rather than running aggressively. Shear or mow the foliage back hard in late winter before new growth emerges to remove tattered old leaves and keep the planting looking fresh for the coming season.
